node.label: Political, international & national history
node.period_rationale: Landmark works date from the 1970s (Granatstein 1975, Whitaker 1977, English 1977, Stacey 1977) through the 1990s, with a post-2000 extension (British World, Bothwell 2007, Chapnick). groups.json gives period_2/period_3; period_2 marks expansion, not an end.
node.date_label: Granatstein 1975, 1977, 1982 · Whitaker 1977 · Stacey 1977–81 · Bothwell, Drummond and English 1981 · Owram 1986 · Buckner 1993 · Whitaker and Marcuse 1994 · British World 2006 · CHA political history prizes first listed 2011 · Heaman's 'new political history' 2017 · coverage through 2000, selected later works

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones; political and diplomatic history of Canada is older (see cdn_national_tradition). 2006 and later dates (the prizes' first listing in 2011, Heaman 2017) are in the partial extension.

node.description: Research on the Canadian state, its parties, officials, wars and foreign relations, and the national syntheses built from them. Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975), of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) and of the Ottawa mandarins (1982), Whitaker's study of the Liberal party and the state (1977) and Owram's history of the intellectuals who argued for planning and reform (1986) examined how federal power was organized, staffed and justified. Stacey's history of external policies (1977, 1981), Hillmer and Granatstein's Empire to Umpire (1994) and Bothwell's Alliance and Illusion (2007) treated Canada's place in the world. Bothwell, Drummond and English's Canada since 1945 (1981) and Thompson and Seager's Centenary Series volume (1985) offered national syntheses; political biography (Brown on Borden, Bélanger on Laurier, English on Pearson) and Bliss's business history kept leaders and enterprise in view. Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1994) turned to the security state. Buckner's 1993 address, asking historians to restore the settlement colonies to imperial history, led to the British World volume (2006). Chapnick (2000, 2005) questioned the middle-power 'golden age'. Granatstein and Bliss also led the national side of the 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate. Since 2011 the CHA's political history prizes have rewarded a 'new political history' of state, tax and governance: Heaman on taxation (2017), Loo on forced relocation (2019), Bohaker on Anishinaabe governance (2020), and francophone studies of Hydro-Québec (Savard) and cultural policy (Harvey) that are recognized but not yet widely cited.
node.scope_note: A research field for the political, diplomatic and national history of the Canadian state, widened to include the 'new political history' of state, tax and governance (Heaman's subtitle) that the CHA's political history prizes have recognized since they were first listed in 2011; business history and the British World are distinct strands. The debate over national history is a separate entry (who_killed_debate, user decision 2026-10-12): Granatstein's and Bliss's polemics are placed there, their scholarship here; Bliss's primary placement is here, with a debate roster row there (Q73, user decision 2026-10-12). Military history is a separate proposed entry (cdn_military); Stacey and Granatstein are shared, not merged. Francophone political history (Bélanger; Savard and Harvey, recognized by CHA prizes but not yet widely cited) is thin in the PhD corpus; Quebec political history belongs mostly to quebec_historiography. Post-2000 works are a partial extension.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Granatstein, Canada's War (1975), Broken Promises (with Hitsman, 1977), The Ottawa Men (1982); Whitaker, The Government Party (1977); English, The Decline of Politics (1977), Shadow of Heaven (1989); Stacey, Canada and the Age of Conflict (1977, 1981); Bothwell, Drummond and English, Canada since 1945 (1981); Thompson and Seager, Canada 1922–1939 (1985); Brown, Robert Laird Borden (1975, 1980); Bélanger, Wilfrid Laurier (1986); Owram, The Government Generation (1986); Bliss, A Living Profit (1974), Northern Enterprise (1987), Right Honourable Men (1994); Drummond, Progress without Planning (1987); Bercuson, True Patriot (1993); Hillmer and Granatstein, Empire to Umpire (1994); Whitaker and Marcuse, Cold War Canada (1994); Buckner, "Whatever Happened to the British Empire?" (1993); Buckner and Francis, eds., Canada and the British World (2006); Bothwell, Alliance and Illusion (2007). Critique: Chapnick (2000, 2005). New political history (prize-recognized, extension): Heaman, Tax, Order, and Good Government (2017); Loo, Moved by the State (2019); Bohaker, Doodem and Council Fire (2020). Francophone (recognized, little cited): Savard (2010, 2013); Harvey, Histoire des politiques culturelles au Québec (2022).

representative_people.name: J. L. Granatstein
representative_people.context: Histories of the King government at war (1975), conscription (with J. M. Hitsman, 1977) and the federal mandarinate (1982); co-author of a survey of Canada's external relations (1994). His 1998 polemic belongs to who_killed_debate.
representative_people.works: Canada's War (1975); Broken Promises (1977); The Ottawa Men (1982); Empire to Umpire (1994, with Hillmer)

representative_people.name: Robert Bothwell
representative_people.context: Co-author of national syntheses of twentieth-century Canada (1981, 1987) and author of a synthesis of Canada's foreign relations, 1945–84 (2007).
representative_people.works: Canada since 1945 (1981, with Drummond and English); Alliance and Illusion (2007)

representative_people.name: John English
representative_people.context: Party-system history (1977), co-authored national synthesis (1981) and political biography of Pearson (1989).
representative_people.works: The Decline of Politics (1977); Canada since 1945 (1981); Shadow of Heaven (1989)

representative_people.name: Ian M. Drummond
representative_people.context: Economic historian of Ontario and co-author of the postwar national synthesis.

representative_people.name: Norman Hillmer
representative_people.context: Historian of Canada's external relations; co-author of Empire to Umpire (1994). Catalogue level only.

representative_people.name: Reg Whitaker
representative_people.context: Studies party and state in the Liberal era (1977, contents checked) and, with Gary Marcuse, the anti-communist "national insecurity state" (1994, description read).

representative_people.name: John Herd Thompson
representative_people.context: Co-author, with Allen Seager, of the Centenary Series volume on 1922–39 (1985).

representative_people.name: Phillip Buckner
representative_people.context: His 1993 address asked historians of empire and of the settler colonies to restore the colonies of settlement to "Greater Britain"; co-editor of Canada and the British World (2006). Also founding editor of Acadiensis (see cdn_regional).
representative_people.works: "Whatever Happened to the British Empire?" (1993); Canada and the British World (2006, with Francis)

representative_people.name: R. Douglas Francis
representative_people.context: Co-editor of Canada and the British World (2006).

representative_people.name: David J. Bercuson

representative_people.name: Adam Chapnick
representative_people.context: Calls Canada's middle-power status "a myth" (2000) and questions the "golden age" of diplomacy that "many historians" located at the founding of the United Nations (2005, description).
representative_people.works: "The Canadian Middle Power Myth" (2000); The Middle Power Project (2005)

strands.title: Party, state and the mandarins
strands.focus: The federal state and those who staffed and argued for it: Granatstein's mandarins, Whitaker's Liberal "government party" (contents: "Party and state in the Liberal era") and Owram's intellectuals of planning and reform.
strands.works: J. L. Granatstein, The Ottawa Men: The Civil Service Mandarins, 1935–1957 (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1982).; Reginald Whitaker, The Government Party: Organizing and Financing the Liberal Party of Canada, 1930–58 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1977).; Doug Owram, The Government Generation: Canadian Intellectuals and the State, 1900–1945 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1986).; John English, The Decline of Politics: The Conservatives and the Party System, 1901–20 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1977).

strands.title: Wartime politics and conscription
strands.focus: The politics of the King government at war and of conscription; overlaps with the military entry.
strands.works: J. L. Granatstein, Canada's War: The Politics of the Mackenzie King Government, 1939–1945 (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1975).; J. L. Granatstein and J. M. Hitsman, Broken Promises: A History of Conscription in Canada (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1977).

strands.title: External policy and international history
strands.focus: From Stacey's external policies to surveys of Canada in the world (Hillmer and Granatstein 1994; Bothwell 2007), with Chapnick's critique of the middle-power story.
strands.works: C. P. Stacey, Canada and the Age of Conflict: A History of Canadian External Policies, vol. 1, 1867–1921 (Toronto: Macmillan, 1977); vol. 2, 1921–1948: The Mackenzie King Era (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1981).; Norman Hillmer and J. L. Granatstein, Empire to Umpire: Canada and the World to the 1990s (Toronto: Copp Clark Longman, 1994).; Robert Bothwell, Alliance and Illusion: Canada and the World, 1945–1984 (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2007).; Adam Chapnick, "The Canadian Middle Power Myth," International Journal 55, no. 2 (2000): 188ff.; Adam Chapnick, The Middle Power Project: Canada and the Founding of the United Nations (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2005).

strands.title: National syntheses of the twentieth century
strands.focus: Textbook syntheses of the twentieth-century state and society.
strands.works: Robert Bothwell, Ian Drummond and John English, Canada since 1945: Power, Politics, and Provincialism (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1981).; John Herd Thompson with Allen Seager, Canada 1922–1939: Decades of Discord, Canadian Centenary Series 15 (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1985).

strands.title: Political biography
strands.focus: Lives of prime ministers and ministers in English and French: Borden, Laurier, Pearson, Claxton, and Bliss's collective study of prime ministers.
strands.works: Robert Craig Brown, Robert Laird Borden: A Biography, vol. 1, 1854–1914 (1975); vol. 2 (1980).; Réal Bélanger, Wilfrid Laurier: quand la politique devient passion (Québec: Presses de l'Université Laval; Montréal: Entreprises Radio-Canada, 1986).; John English, Shadow of Heaven: The Life of Lester Pearson, vol. 1, 1897–1948 (Toronto: Lester & Orpen Dennys, 1989).; David J. Bercuson, True Patriot: The Life of Brooke Claxton, 1898–1960 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1993).; Michael Bliss, Right Honourable Men: The Descent of Canadian Politics from Macdonald to Mulroney (Toronto: HarperCollins, 1994).

strands.title: Business and economic history
strands.focus: Bliss's social history of business and his national business synthesis; Drummond's Ontario economic history. Kept as a strand, not a separate group (Q72): business history is small and falling (47 PhDs, 4.2% → 3.2%).
strands.works: Michael Bliss, A Living Profit: Studies in the Social History of Canadian Business, 1883–1911 (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1974).; Michael Bliss, A Canadian Millionaire: The Life and Business Times of Sir Joseph Flavelle, Bart., 1858–1939 (Toronto: Macmillan of Canada, 1978).; Michael Bliss, Northern Enterprise: Five Centuries of Canadian Business (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1987).; Ian M. Drummond, Progress without Planning: The Economic History of Ontario from Confederation to the Second World War (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1987).

strands.title: The Cold War security state
strands.focus: Whitaker and Marcuse on anti-communist purges, spy scandals and security screening (description read).
strands.works: Reg Whitaker and Gary Marcuse, Cold War Canada: The Making of a National Insecurity State, 1945–1957 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1994).

strands.title: Empire and the British World
strands.focus: Buckner's 1993 call to restore the settlement colonies to imperial history, and the British World volume that surveys Canada's history "through a British lens" while eschewing nostalgia.
strands.works: Phillip Buckner, "Presidential Address: Whatever Happened to the British Empire?" Journal of the Canadian Historical Association 4, no. 1 (1993): 3–32.; Phillip Buckner and R. Douglas Francis, eds., Canada and the British World: Culture, Migration, and Identity (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2006).

strands.title: State, tax and governance: a 'new political history'
strands.focus: Political history as the profession's prizes now recognize it (CHA political history prizes, first listed 2011): Heaman's Tax, Order, and Good Government (2017; best book 2018) on how the fiscal regime was made and received, from a fiscal imperial to a fiscal welfare state; Loo's Moved by the State (2019; 2020) on forced relocation and citizen participation; Bohaker's Doodem and Council Fire (2020; 2021) on Anishinaabe governance through alliance. All post-2000 (extension). The citation-based anchors (Granatstein, Bothwell, English) represent the older diplomatic and political synthesis; these books are newer and their uptake is rising (7–12 PhDs each, mostly since 2020).
strands.works: E. A. Heaman, Tax, Order, and Good Government: A New Political History of Canada, 1867–1917 (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 2017).; Tina Loo, Moved by the State: Forced Relocation and Making a Good Life in Postwar Canada (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2019).; Heidi Bohaker, Doodem and Council Fire: Anishinaabe Governance through Alliance (Toronto: Osgoode Society for Canadian Legal History and University of Toronto Press, 2020).

strands.title: Francophone political history: recognized, not yet widely cited
strands.focus: The CHA's French-language political history article prize (first listed 2012) and its book prize have recognized francophone histories of the Quebec state: Savard on Hydro-Québec under the Union nationale (article prize 2012; book 2013) and Harvey's history of Quebec cultural policy, 1855–1976 (best book 2023). PhD uptake is still low (Savard's chapter 1 PhD and book 5, 2009–2026; Harvey none yet), so they mark recognition rather than use. Bélanger's Laurier (1986) is the pre-2000 francophone political work here. Post-2000 works are extension.
strands.works: Stéphane Savard, « L’instrumentalisation d’Hydro-Québec par l’Union nationale (1944-1960) : quels rôles pour le développement hydroélectrique? », in Xavier Gélinas and Lucia Ferretti, eds., Duplessis, son milieu, son époque (Québec: Septentrion, 2010).; Stéphane Savard, Hydro-Québec et l’État québécois, 1944–2005 (Québec: Septentrion, 2013).; Fernand Harvey, Histoire des politiques culturelles au Québec, 1855–1976 (Québec: Septentrion, 2022).

uptake.note: Falling: 23.7% (2009–14) → 10.4% (2020–26), the steepest fall of the four drafts. Most-cited works here: Whitaker and Marcuse, Cold War Canada (50 PhDs); Owram, Government Generation (39); Granatstein, Ottawa Men (36); Stacey, Age of Conflict (35); Bothwell, Alliance and Illusion (34). Of the people, Granatstein is cited by 161 PhDs, but his share falls from 15.4% to 7.6%.

relation_to_periods: Main period: landmark works 1975–1994 fall in period_2/period_3. The British World volume (2006), Bothwell (2007), Chapnick (2005) and the prize-recognized new political and francophone political history (Savard 2010, 2013; Heaman 2017; Loo 2019; Bohaker 2020; Harvey 2022) are partial extension. Engagement in 2009–2026 PhDs falls from 23.7% to 10.4%.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Canadian political history of party, state and officials
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: A Canadian case of the atlas field: Whitaker's Government Party (contents: "The national Liberal party, 1930–58"; "Party and state in the Liberal era") and Owram's Government Generation (description: intellectuals and the planning of the welfare state, 1900–45) study institutions and the people who ran and justified them. Comparison: the atlas entry is international and methodologically plural; the Canadian field is not presented as a branch of Namier or Tilly.

proposed_relationships.relationship: From national tradition to a specialized political and international history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) places Stacey with Creighton among the conservative nationalists who took the nation-state as their frame; Stacey's external-policy history (1977, 1981) is the most-cited external-policy work in this draft. Thompson and Seager's volume (1985) belongs to the Centenary Series. Comparison only: no lineage of teachers and students is asserted. PhD context: 118 of 242 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with cdn_political_national also engage the cdn_national_tradition anchor set (49% vs 13% of all; lift 3.67). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Canada and the British World: imperial history from the settler colonies
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Buckner (1993, abstract) argues that historians of the second British Empire neglect the colonies of settlement and Pocock's "Greater Britain", and that historians of the settler colonies share the blame; Canada and the British World (2006) surveys Canadian history "through a British lens" while eschewing nostalgia. The atlas has no separate imperial-history entry; nationaltradition (national and imperial narratives) is the nearest. Comparison, scoped to the British World strand.

proposed_relationships.relationship: War policy, conscription and the state
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Stacey's official history of war policy (1970) and Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975) and of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) sit between political and military history. Metadata-level only: no abstract or contents page was read for these books. PhD context: 142 of 242 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with cdn_political_national also engage the cdn_military anchor set (59% vs 14% of all; lift 4.16). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.
proposed_relationships.merge_note: Same pair and kind as milreq_rel_06 in the cdn_military draft (Stacey 1970, Morton 1981). Accept one edge carrying both source sets.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: Bliss's business history and Drummond's Ontario economic history; only catalogue and review headers seen. Business history stays a strand here (Q72); no checked source yet ties it to the atlas economic entry.
Buckner's British World concerns colonies of settlement, but its relation to settler-colonial analysis is not stated in any checked source. Lift 1.94 only.
High PhD overlap (lift 3.67, mainly Owram, Whitaker and Bothwell) but no checked text links the fields. Leave to the cdn_sixties draft.
